body:
# Nafanua — the one true spelling, and the forms that fail it

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Nafanua, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Nafanua to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The tradition's record preserves this name in its romanized scholarly form: **Nafanua** — no older script survives to transcribe, so the canonical content is the exactness of the spelling itself.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: 'nah-fah-NOO-ah' — stress falls on the penultimate syllable as in all Sāmoan words; every syllable is open and clean. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *nafanua* differs from the canonical *Nafanua* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. When the London Missionary Society's teachers landed in the 1830s, Sāmoan orators already had a frame ready for them: Nafanua's prophecy of a government from the west, recorded decades earlier by Stair, was reinterpreted in village talk as foretelling the new faith and the new order arriving across the sea.  The tradition was never flattened into Christianity — she remains a goddess, not a saint — but her prophecy gave the conversion an indigenous grammar of expectation, letting Samoa receive the missionaries as the fulfillment of its own story rather than a rupture.

And it never stopped working. Nafanua endures in Samoa as the patroness of just rebellion and the archetype of the woman who rules.  The village of Falealupo on Savai'i keeps her story on its own ground — the site of the earth that hid her and the battlefield that raised her — and Sāmoan orators still invoke her in speeches about legitimate government, the malo.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: vowel-length marking as the language commissions standardize it. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## Where Protocol Meets Practice

The technical answer is simple: the canonical marks are legal IDNA 2008 characters, encoded as punycode under `xn--`. The practical answer is messier: legal does not mean stocked (registrar inventory is partial), and stocked does not mean typeable (stacked diacritics defeat mobile keyboards).

So the register's rule is a hierarchy of attested forms — full restoration, circumflex, macron-only, attested variant, and finally plain ASCII for the systems that cannot carry marks. Every rung is defensible because every rung is attested. The forms this register rules against are not rungs; they are errors, and errors do not get rungs.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Nafanua** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *nafanua* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Nafanua** stands at [/nafanua/](/nafanua/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 5 cited sources — Turner, George, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before (1884), Stair, John B., Old Samoa or Flotsam and Jetsam from the Pacific Ocean (1897), Kramer, Augustin, The Samoa Islands (1902).
